OBJ.why: Step 1: a `persisted` write commits by one conditional PUT to the object store (R `obj`, Q `put`). Step 2: that PUT costs p99 2.67 ms on local MinIO, but about 30 ms typical on S3 Standard and at or above 7.3 ms p99 on Express One Zone (cited in E-28). Step 3: the bar is C + 5 ms = 5.7 ms here, so on any real store the write p99 is over it; E-28's own threshold puts OBJ out at `persisted`.

V4.why: Step 1: in v4 any member writes, and cells merge by last-writer-wins on Lamport stamps (R `lww`; O `lamp` is 'no total order per partition' in SPACE §2). Step 2: so there is no committed log per partition, and two members can apply two writes in different orders. Step 3: P-01 asks for per-partition order, and its test 'every replica's rows equal the fold of the committed log' cannot be stated for v4.

BUY.why: On JetStream with fsync on three replicas, 900 writes through a leader kill lost nothing, read-your-writes held 900 of 900 and a held row read in 81 ns (E-44); a single ack takes p99 1.31 ms (E-09b). No seeded sweep can run on nats-server's bytes, and the write pin under load was not timed.
BUY.closes: The pattern's check on a JetStream cluster; no seeded sim is possible there (TEST-10).

V4.why: Step 1: P-02 wants every copy to agree which rows exist at each log position, with expiry inside one tick + `skew.max` of one clock. Step 2: v4 has no writer time (T is empty in SPACE §4) and no log position per partition (O `lamp`); each member would expire by its own clock and merge by last-writer-wins. Step 3: so a `touch` on one member and an expiry on another race, and copies can disagree; fixing it needs another row's T and R options.

BUY.why: Not tried on JetStream (E-44 ran P-01, P-09, P-10 and P-14 only). JetStream 2.10 expires by stream age, with no record for a follower to fold, so per-row `ttl` and `touch` need an expirer process that nobody built.

default.why: With the `END` fix (A-06), E-31's model of subscribe holds every property (a snapshot then deltas with no gap and no overlap, a cursor that never goes back, own writes visible) on ten bounds explored in full, up to 7.6 million states: a leader crash, a reload, a dropped link, a slot move and a relay. E-22's near-cache check (a one-hop miss, `shortfall`, the memory bound) passes 100 of 100 seeds in three modes. A client cursor is 22 to 79 B (E-19).

CELL.why: Cells move whole, so group offsets keep their meaning (E-31's `off` option holds on every bound with no move). At a re-key the model refuses a cursor of the old generation and restarts the reader from a snapshot (E-17c, 6 rules): for a state follower that is a snapshot, then deltas, with nothing missed. The near-cache library is E-22's.

LANE.why: No partition moves between lanes in this row, and E-31's `off` option (group offsets) holds every property on every bound without a move. The near-cache library is E-22's.

SPLIT.why: Offsets with lineage: E-17b and E-17c model a reader across a split and a merge and hold with 2 to 3 lineage rules, and E-31's protocol holds on the bounds without a move. The two were not run in one model. The near-cache library is E-22's.

ISR.why: Fixed partitions never move, so offsets keep their meaning, and E-31's `off` option holds every property on every bound without a move; serving from a follower at a position is Kafka's KIP-392, E-31's own precedent. The in-sync-set commit rule itself was not modelled.

PD.why: E-31 modelled per-slot sequences and group offsets, served from any ready replica. This row has timestamps (O `hlc`) and lease or read-index reads only (no W `any`), so its follow path has no model here.
PD.closes: E-31's model with this row's positions and read paths.

V4.why: v4 follows by digests and Lamport stamps, not cursors, so P-03's cursor property has no form to check. DESIGN-V5 §9 measured a client that opened one room's server view holding all 1,000 rows.
V4.closes: Nothing is planned: V4 is the reference row and takes no fix.

CELL.why: Step 1: CELL's positions are group offsets (O `off`), and it grows by a re-key that copies rows into a new generation of groups. Step 2: as written, a cursor of the old generation is refused `unknown-log` and the reader restarts from a snapshot (E-17c's model; SPACE §2 `rekey`: 'cursors break'); kept without the refusal, offsets give a false `expired` in 5 steps (E-31, `off`). Step 3: so a log reader cannot go on from a kept position after the resource grows: it skips records or reads them again, against 'a position never changes meaning across scaling' and 'every record once, in order'.

V4.why: Step 1: a replayable stream needs one order of records per partition and a position in it. Step 2: v4 keeps a log per origin, compacts it, and stamps cells with Lamport clocks (O `lamp`: no total order per partition). Step 3: so there is no position a reader can replay from that means the same on every member.

Step 2: v4 has no single judge (R `lww`: no conditions or ops, SPACE §5) and no writer time (T is empty); DESIGN-V5 §9 measured two claims that both committed. default.why: On the prototype a delayed message was never claimed before its time by writer time, with the writer's clock skewed 200 ms and a leader change; the cron message came due at 06:00; a waiting take appended nothing (E-22, simulated). Open: the wake came 3.5 ms of virtual time after the enqueue's ack, which is not a pin for 'C + one hop'. And `delay` counts from the adder's clock until the writer stamps it (E-22, D5).
default.closes: The waiting-take wake pin on a real kernel, and a writer-stamped `delay`, in the phase that builds the queue library.

V4.why: Step 1: 'takeable within one tick of its time by the writer's clock' and a take with a lease need writer time and `claim` at one writer. Step 2: v4 has neither (T is empty; R `lww` has no conditions, SPACE §5). Step 3: so two members can hand out one delayed message, each by its own clock.
